newsitem.title: CHINA: China's Jiang Zemin comes under fire from leftists.
newsitem.headline: China's Jiang Zemin comes under fire from leftists.

text.p: China's Communist Party General Secretary Jiang Zemin has come under fire from ultra-leftists just as his mentor paramount leader Deng Xiaoping has died, Chinese analysts said on Saturday.
The February issue of China's most conservative magazine, Zhongliu, or Mainstay, attacked a book seen as pro-Jiang and titled "Talking Heart to Heart with the General Secretary".
"It was the first cannon fired by leftists at Jiang Zemin," a political analyst said of the magazine, mouthpiece of hardliners in the ruling party.
"Jiang Zemin's feathers are not yet full-grown... This could harm him," said the analyst who asked not to be identified.
"It's an open challenge to Jiang Zemin," he said.
The veiled attack on Jiang came in an issue published as Deng lay on his deathbed.

Deng, who died in Beijing on Wednesday aged 92, chose Jiang as his heir in 1989 after the army crushed student-led demonstrations for democracy in Beijing and he sacked the incumbent party chief, Zhao Ziyang, for sympathising with the protesters.

While the power shift so far has been seamless, analysts said upheavals were possible -- especially with Jiang's post as Communist Party chief up for re-election at the 15th Party Congress later this year.
In China's arcane political world, power struggles are fought behind the scenes and traditionally emerge into the public eye only when they erupt on the state media.

Zhongliu magazine questioned the motives of Liu Ji, vice-president of the important Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and author of the book's foreword, and charged the volume "opposed what the party had always advocated".
Liu is believed to be close to Jiang, and in China attacks on members of the party's highest echelons are often oblique, striking at the protege of a leader.
The book omitted to support the cardinal principles laid down by Deng as the basis of communist rule -- such as the leadership of the Communist Party and adhering to socialism.
The magazine slammed the book of essays on Jiang's ideology for suggesting that China's authorities should tolerate or shelter hostile foreign ideological forces instead of locking them out.
"If... we 'tolerate' or 'shelter' hostile ideology trying to overthrow us, it will inevitably lead to the destruction of our socialist ideology and culture," the magazine warned.

The magazine is believed to be close to retired conservative ideologue Deng Liqun, a former speechwriter for Deng Xiaoping until their relations soured due to his opposition to reform. Deng Liqun was sidelined by Jiang.
In a surprise omission, Deng Liqun was not included in the 459-member Funeral Committee formed after Deng Xiaoping's death -- a "who's who" of who is in and who is out in Chinese politics.
The language used by the magazine was reminiscent of the chaotic 1966-76 Cultural Revolution that Mao Zedong used to purge his opponents, analysts said.
"The magazine is trying to stir up debate reminiscent of the Cultural Revolution... to oust Jiang Zemin," one said.
Some Western diplomats see Jiang as a transitional figure even though he has China's three top jobs of party chief, state president and head of the armed forces.
Since imperial China, social convulsions and power struggles have often accompanied the transfer of the "mandate of heaven" to a new emperor -- or party chief.
An editor of the magazine declined to comment on whether the article was an attack on Jiang.
Delivery of the magazine has been delayed by more than one week and it was unavailable on the market. Officials blamed the delay on the lunar New Year holiday this month.
